Q: Why does wildcard not work in (the prerequisites of) a static pattern rule? A:

Why do wildcards not work the same in the static pattern rule?

The manual does not speak directly to the question. However, I observe that make is not itself a shell, and its support for wildcards is its own. Really its own, in the sense that the POSIX specifications for make do not define any behavior for them, yet warn that some implementations may do. GNU make does its own idiosyncratic thing here.

I note also that the GNU make manual introduces wildcards by saying "A single file name can specify many files using wildcard characters" (emphasis added). The patterns in pattern rules are exactly that -- patterns -- not file names. I acknowledge that that's a fine distinction to draw, but if you want an explanation based on the manual then I don't think there's better one available.

Other than that, there are pragmatic reasons for make not to combine wildcards with pattern matching, but no technical reason why it couldn't do.

Q: How to adjust CSS via media query to a dynamically set orientation during printing? A:

Why that's not a bug but a feature:

https://www.w3.org/TR/css-page-3/#page-size

If a size property declaration is qualified by a width, height, device-width, device-height, aspect-ratio, device-aspect-ratio or orientation media query (or other conditional on the size of the paper), then the declaration must be ignored. Media queries do not honor size: they assume the paper size that would be chosen if no @page rules were specified.

In short, the very last sentence clearly states:

Media queries do not honor size: they assume the paper size that would be chosen if no @page rules were specified.

So this is not a browser bug — it is actually the specified behavior. Media queries are deliberately designed to ignore @page { size }. They evaluate against the UA's default paper size as if no @page rules existed at all.

Interestingly, the spec itself acknowledges this is unsatisfactory. Right after that rule there's an editorial note saying:

It would be useful if media queries could respond at least to sizes specified on an unqualified @page.

The circularity issue (the @page size depending on the media query, and the media query depending on the @page size) is maybe why they punted and said media queries simply don't see @page size at all.

Anyway even if the case discussed here in this question doesn't hold any ambiguity, yet it's dismissed by the general rule.

How to handle it:

Now to properly answer the question you asked in the title:

How to adjust CSS based on orientation during printing?

With the question stated as that, the way you did it's exactly the right way:

@media print and (orientation: landscape) { /* your style */ }

But it will work only as long as the orientation is not coming from the @page size rule since it won't be honored, but it's decided by the user through the print dialog.

It's important to stress that if you have a @page size rule, it will specify a page orientation whether you did it or not, and it will force that one, preventing the user to pick its custom choice. If that value won't match with the UA default value, it won't be honored by the media query preventing the style to be applied. That's true because the rule to evaluate media queries, like if no @page rules existed at all, still stands.

That's why this styling would work instead:

@page { size: a4 portrait; }
@media print and (orientation: portrait) { /* your style */ }

Because the media query is not honoring the @page size rule but just because it happens to match with the UA default and despite you forced the orientation preventing to user to pick another one, it still matches with the orientation that the media query is going to honor (the UA default and not strictly the @page size).

So how would you achieve your goal to force the paper orientation during printing and yet having that specific style?

Just specify the @page size: landscape rule and strip off the orientation condition from the media query so you won't hit that case where it will fail since it can't honor the @page size and be dimissed:

@page { size: a4 landscape; }
@media print { /* your style */ }

Don't forget that saying you want landscape orientation will prevent the user to pick the portrait option so it's pointless to support a different style since portrait can't occur anymore.

I did my best covering every single edge case but if something wasn't clear already and you are still asking:

But why is the media query applied correctly when the @page rule is omitted and the orientation is selected manually?

The media query has a condition:

@media print and (orientation: `<portrait|landscape>`)

If @page rule was omitted:

  • The printing page orientation can be chosen from the print dialog;
  • The media query condition will honor the orientation picked in the print dialog and will kick in if it does match, and it won't if it doesn't;

If @page { size } was used:

  • The printing page orientation will be forced in the print dialog;
  • The print dialog won't allow you to pick a different orientation;
  • The media query condition and (orientation: <portrait|landscape>) won't honor the orientation specified (for the css spec said earlier) and it will kick in only if the condition happens to match the default orientation owned by the browser. So the media query will work in 99% of the cases (I would say 100%) ONLY if you used: and (orientation: portrait), or if you omitted the condition entirely;
  • The media query won't ever kick in if the condition is landscape because by css spec it's not meant to honor the @page rule AND I wonder if there's any scenario where landscape is default;

When will the media query kick in:

  • ONLY when its condition is met because the orientation is matching what comes from the user selected choice or what comes from the browser's default orientation. If you used a @page rule, you will force the print dialog having a fixed orientation and you will prevent it to come from the user preference so you'll be left only with the browser's default as the truth to match your condition against with.

Q: Using the Google Maps API, how can I retrieve the name of a building with only the street address? A:

The Google Maps APIs, much like Google Maps itself, will return the address itself rather than a business at the address, when the query is the address. This is the intended behavior as explained in https://issuetracker.google.com/118784707

The functionality of showing a list of businesses at an address, as additional data for the address itself, has never been available in any of the Google Maps APIs. As a workaround, Place Nearby Search may be used to find the nearest establishments ranked by distance, bearing in mind even the closest ones may not always have the same address.

Q: How to handle FileNotFoundError when "try .. except IOError" does not catch it? A:

FileNotFoundError is a subclass of OSError, catch that or the exception itself:

except OSError as e:

Operating System exceptions have been reworked in Python 3.3; FileNotFoundError was added, and IOError has been merged into OSError. See the PEP 3151: Reworking the OS and IO exception hierarchy section in the What's New documentation.

For more details the OS Exceptions section for more information, scroll down for a class hierarchy.

That said, your code should still just work as IOError is now an alias for OSError:

>>> IOError
<class 'OSError'>

Make sure you are placing your exception handler in the correct location. Take a close look at the traceback for the exception to make sure you didn't miss where it is actually being raised. Last but not least, you did restart your Python script, right?
